name: Wireless Architectures
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Compare AP architectures and modes, wire APs and WLCs, and read AireOS and Catalyst 9800 WLAN pages: general, security, QoS, advanced.

lesson.intro: Wireless clients need a design behind the radios. Compare autonomous, cloud-managed and controller-based APs, learn how APs and WLCs plug into the switched network, and read the WLAN pages of the AireOS and Catalyst 9800 GUIs the exam shows.
objectives: Compare autonomous, cloud-based and lightweight AP architectures and WLC deployments
Choose the right AP mode, from local and FlexConnect to monitor and SE-Connect
Describe how APs and WLCs connect to switches: access ports, trunks, LAG and PoE
Interpret AireOS WLAN settings on the General, Security, QoS and Advanced tabs
Map them onto Catalyst 9800 profiles and tags, and troubleshoot a client that cannot join

sections.title: Autonomous, cloud-based and lightweight APs
sections.key: Autonomous APs are configured one by one and trunked, cloud-based APs are run from a cloud dashboard with local data, and lightweight APs depend on a WLC.
sections.body:
An access point bridges wireless clients onto the wired network. The architecture question is where the AP's brain lives.

An **autonomous AP** holds its own SSIDs, VLAN mappings, security, channel and power. With 500 of them, every client VLAN stretches to every AP and every change is made 500 times.

A **cloud-based AP** (Cisco Meraki) forwards traffic like an autonomous AP but pulls its configuration from the vendor's cloud at boot. Only management and monitoring go to the cloud; client data stays local.

A **lightweight AP** hands most of its work to a **wireless LAN controller (WLC)** and cannot normally work without one.

[[visual]]

items.title: Autonomous
points: Configured one AP at a time (console, SSH, HTTPS) through a management IP
Maps each SSID to a wired VLAN itself
Switch port: a trunk with the management and client VLANs

items.title: Cloud-based
points: One cloud dashboard for every site
The cloud pushes configuration and firmware, tunes channels and power, tracks rogues
Client data goes from the AP straight onto the local network

items.title: Lightweight
points: Configured and managed by a WLC
Tunnels client traffic to the WLC with CAPWAP

sections.pitfall: Thinking cloud-managed means client traffic travels through the cloud. Only management and monitoring go to the cloud; user data stays local.

check.question: Which AP architecture is configured one AP at a time and needs a trunk to each AP because the AP itself maps SSIDs to VLANs?
choices: Cloud-based APs managed from a dashboard
check.explanation: Autonomous APs carry their own configuration, so each is managed separately, and they put client traffic directly onto VLANs, which requires a trunk. Lightweight APs tunnel traffic to a WLC, and cloud-based APs are configured centrally.

sections.title: Split MAC and CAPWAP
sections.key: Split MAC keeps real-time 802.11 work on the AP and management on the WLC, joined by CAPWAP tunnels: control on UDP 5246, data on UDP 5247.
sections.body:
A lightweight AP keeps only the jobs that must happen in real time at the radio and moves the rest to the WLC. That is the **split-MAC architecture**.

[[visual]]

The two talk through **CAPWAP**, an IETF standard (RFC 5415) based on Cisco's older **LWAPP**. It builds two tunnels between the AP's IP address and the WLC's management interface:

[[visual 2]]

CAPWAP is ordinary IP, so the AP and WLC can sit in different subnets or buildings; the tunnels are simply routed. Client VLANs live at the WLC, so the AP needs one IP address and an access port. AP and WLC authenticate each other with X.509 certificates.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: CAPWAP tunnels
rows: AP configuration and management; always authenticated and encrypted with DTLS
Client traffic to and from the WLC; DTLS encryption optional, off by default

visual.title: A new lightweight AP comes online

steps.label: Discovers WLC addresses
steps.detail: DHCP option 43, a DNS lookup of CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER, a subnet broadcast, or a WLC it joined before

sections.deeper: Once its APs have joined, the WLC tunes the whole wireless network centrally: dynamic channel assignment, transmit power optimization, self-healing coverage when an AP dies, fast roaming between APs, client load balancing, RF monitoring and wireless intrusion protection. That central view is the real payoff of split MAC.
sections.pitfall: Mixing up the ports. Control is 5246 and data is 5247: control comes first.

check.question: Which statement about CAPWAP is true?
choices: It uses TCP 5246 for data and TCP 5247 for control
It requires the AP and WLC to be in the same VLAN
It uses UDP 5246 for control and UDP 5247 for data between a lightweight AP and its WLC
It carries only management traffic; client data is always switched at the AP
check.explanation: CAPWAP runs over UDP: 5246 for the control tunnel and 5247 for the data tunnel. Because the tunnels are routed IP packets, the AP and WLC can be in different subnets, and in local mode client data rides the data tunnel.

sections.title: Where the controller lives
sections.key: WLC deployment models are unified (central, about 6000 APs), cloud-based VM (about 3000), embedded in a switch stack (about 200) and Mobility Express on an AP (about 100).
sections.body:
Split MAC works wherever the WLC sits. The official guide's typical maximums vary by model; the relative sizes are what matter:

[[visual]]

Do not confuse a **cloud-based WLC** (a controller VM in your own data center, still running CAPWAP to its APs) with **cloud-based APs** such as Meraki (no WLC at all). The exam likes that trap.

Branches add a twist. If a store's APs tunnel every packet to a WLC at headquarters, local traffic crosses the WAN twice, and a WAN outage stops the store's Wi-Fi. The FlexConnect AP mode, next, solves both.

rows: As a hardware WLC in the core or data center
As a virtual machine in a data center or private cloud
On one of the site's APs
visual.caption: Cisco's newer equivalent of Mobility Express is the Embedded Wireless Controller on Catalyst APs.

sections.pitfall: Confusing "cloud-based WLC" with "cloud-based APs". The first is still a controller with CAPWAP tunnels, just virtualized; the second has no controller at all.

check.question: A small campus wants the controller function to run inside its access-layer switch stack. Which deployment model is that?
check.explanation: An embedded WLC runs within the switching hardware at the access layer. Unified is a central appliance, cloud-based is a virtual machine in a data center, and Mobility Express runs on an AP.

sections.title: AP modes
sections.key: Local mode (the default) and FlexConnect serve clients; monitor, sniffer, rogue detector and SE-Connect are dedicated tools; bridge links sites or builds a mesh.
sections.body:
From the WLC you can give a lightweight AP a specific job:

[[visual]]

The tool modes (monitor, sniffer, rogue detector, SE-Connect) stop the AP from serving clients. If a question says the AP must keep serving users, the answer is local or FlexConnect.

Where is the mode set? On AireOS, under Wireless > Access Points > All APs > AP Mode. On a Catalyst 9800, local versus FlexConnect follows the AP's **site tag** (Enable Local Site off means FlexConnect), while monitor, sniffer and bridge are set on the AP itself.

rows: Normal campus client service. Tunnels traffic to the WLC and, in idle moments, scans other channels for noise, rogues and IDS events
Branches across a WAN: switches client traffic locally and keeps serving clients if the link to the WLC fails
Never transmits: a dedicated IDS, rogue detection and location sensor
Captures 802.11 frames and sends them to an analyzer such as Wireshark
Correlates MACs seen on the wired network with rogues heard over the air
Spectrum analysis on all channels to find non-Wi-Fi interference such as microwave ovens
Point-to-point or multipoint links between sites, or a mesh. Flex+Bridge combines it with FlexConnect

sections.pitfall: Choosing monitor mode for an AP that must also serve users. Monitor never transmits, so no client can associate to it.

check.question: A retail branch connects to headquarters over a WAN. Its APs must keep serving clients if the WAN link to the central WLC fails. Which AP mode fits?
check.explanation: FlexConnect APs can switch traffic locally and continue serving clients without the WLC. A local-mode AP depends on its CAPWAP tunnel, and monitor and SE-Connect do not serve clients at all.

sections.title: Wiring APs: access ports, trunks and PoE
sections.key: A local-mode lightweight AP needs only an access port because every WLAN rides CAPWAP; autonomous and locally switching FlexConnect APs need 802.1Q trunks.
sections.body:
Wireless only replaces the last few meters. How an AP plugs in depends on where its client traffic leaves the AP:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Most APs draw **Power over Ethernet (PoE)** from the switch, the power sourcing equipment (PSE); the AP is the powered device (PD).

[[visual 2]]

An AP that gets less power than it wants may boot with radios or features disabled. Enable PortFast on AP access ports, and keep CDP or LLDP on: APs use them to negotiate power.

rows: Every WLAN, whatever its VLAN, rides the CAPWAP tunnel from one IP address to the WLC
It drops client traffic onto local VLANs; its management VLAN is usually native
It maps each SSID to a wired VLAN itself

sections.code:
! Lightweight AP, local mode: access port
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 description LAP-Floor2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 50
 spanning-tree portfast
!
! FlexConnect AP switching locally (or autonomous AP): trunk
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/11
 description FlexAP-Branch
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 50
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 50,100,200
 spanning-tree portfast trunk
sections.deeper: The official guide offers a neat way to see it: the wireless side of an AP already "trunks" 802.11 frames by marking each with the BSSID of the WLAN it belongs to. The only question is whether the wired side needs 802.1Q tags as well, and that depends on whether the AP or the WLC puts client traffic onto VLANs.
sections.pitfall: Trunking every AP port "just in case". A local-mode AP sends only untagged CAPWAP traffic, so a trunk adds nothing but exposure; match the port to where client traffic leaves the AP.

check.question: How should the switch port connected to a lightweight AP in local mode normally be configured?
choices: As an access port in the AP's VLAN
As a trunk carrying every client VLAN
As a routed port with no switchport
As an EtherChannel member using LACP
check.explanation: In local mode all WLAN traffic rides the CAPWAP tunnel from the AP's single IP address, so an access port is enough. The WLC's distribution ports, not the AP, connect to the client VLANs.

sections.title: WLC ports, interfaces and LAG
sections.key: WLC distribution system ports carry CAPWAP and client VLANs on 802.1Q trunks, often in a LAG that needs mode on; the service port is out-of-band on an access port.
sections.body:
On a controller, **ports** are physical connections and **interfaces** are logical Layer 3 identities.

[[visual]]

Distribution ports can be bundled into a **LAG**: one logical link, like an EtherChannel, that survives a member failure. AireOS does not negotiate LACP or PAgP, so the switch side uses `channel-group N mode on`.

[[code]]

[[visual 2]]

A **Catalyst 9800** runs IOS XE, so it looks like a switch: trunk ports (a port-channel can negotiate LACP), an SVI as the wireless management interface, client VLANs as ordinary VLANs, and a separate out-of-band management port.

visual.title: AireOS WLC ports
rows: Out-of-band management, initial setup and recovery; one VLAN
CAPWAP from APs, client data into wired VLANs, in-band management (HTTPS, SSH, SNMP, RADIUS)
Serial CLI: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit
Links a peer WLC for high availability

visual.title: AireOS WLC interfaces
rows: Management traffic (SSH, HTTPS, SNMP, RADIUS, NTP, syslog); terminates CAPWAP
Non-routed address for client DHCP relay, web authentication and mobility; often 192.0.2.1, the same on every controller in a mobility group
Management address of an HA pair
Maps a WLAN to a VLAN, with its own IP address, gateway and DHCP servers

sections.code:
! Switch side of an AireOS WLC
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/46
 description WLC1 service port
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 99
!
interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/47 - 48
 description WLC1 distribution system ports (LAG)
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 50,100,200
 channel-group 5 mode on
sections.pitfall: Configuring LACP active toward an AireOS WLC's LAG. The controller never answers, so no channel forms. Use mode on (a Catalyst 9800 can negotiate LACP).

check.question: Which WLC port connects to a switch trunk and carries CAPWAP tunnels and client traffic?
check.explanation: Distribution system ports carry all normal traffic in many VLANs, so they connect to 802.1Q trunks. The service port is for out-of-band management on one VLAN, the console is serial, and the redundancy port links an HA peer.

sections.title: Creating a WLAN in the WLC GUI
sections.key: On AireOS, create a dynamic interface for the VLAN, then WLANs > Create New > Go, and on the General tab enable the WLAN and bind it to that interface.
sections.body:
Exam screenshots mostly show the classic AireOS GUI. Browse with HTTPS to the WLC's management address and click **Advanced** for the full GUI: tabs Monitor, WLANs, Controller, Wireless, Security, Management, Commands and Help.

The example builds an Engineering WLAN for VLAN 100. Have three answers ready first: the SSID, the interface and VLAN, and the security type.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Keep WLANs few. A controller supports 512 and an AP advertises at most 16, but every SSID's beacons cost airtime; aim for three to five.

steps.label: Enterprise only: add the RADIUS server
steps.detail: Security > AAA > RADIUS > Authentication > New: IP address, shared secret, port 1812, Network User and/or Management

steps.label: Create a dynamic interface
steps.detail: Controller > Interfaces > New: name, VLAN ID 100, IP address, netmask, gateway, DHCP servers

steps.label: Create the WLAN
steps.detail: WLANs > Create New > Go: type, profile name, SSID and ID (an index local to this controller)

steps.label: Set the General, Security, QoS and Advanced tabs, then Apply

visual.title: General tab
rows: Tick Enabled, or the WLAN is never advertised
Read-only summary of the Security tab (default WPA2 with 802.1X)
All by default, or one band: 802.11a only (5 GHz) or 802.11b/g only (2.4 GHz)
The dynamic interface, which decides the clients' VLAN. The default is management, a common mistake
Puts the SSID in beacons; hiding it adds no real security

sections.pitfall: Leaving Interface/Interface Group on management. Clients then land in the management VLAN and get addresses from the wrong subnet, or none at all.

activity.title: Create the Staff WLAN
activity.prompt: Use the simulated controller to build the Staff WLAN from scratch: create it with the SSID Staff, enable it, bind it to the existing staff interface (VLAN 20), secure it with WPA2, AES and a pre-shared key, and give it the Gold QoS profile. Apply, then run the client test and confirm the laptop gets an address in VLAN 20.

check.question: On a WLAN's General tab, which setting determines the VLAN that wireless clients' traffic is placed in on the wired network?
check.explanation: The WLAN is bound to a dynamic interface, and that interface is tied to a VLAN. Radio Policy chooses bands, Broadcast SSID controls beacons, and the profile name is just a label.

sections.title: The Security tab: Layer 2, Layer 3 and AAA servers
sections.key: Layer 2 security sets authentication and encryption: WPA2 with AES plus PSK is Personal, plus 802.1X is Enterprise, and WPA3-Personal needs SAE with PMF Required.
sections.body:
The Security tab decides how clients prove who they are and how frames are encrypted. It has three sub-tabs.

**Layer 2** holds the Layer 2 Security drop-down: None (open), WPA+WPA2, 802.1X (dynamic WEP), Static WEP and legacy options. Choose WPA+WPA2 or a WPA3 option, and avoid anything with WEP.

[[visual]]

**Layer 3** adds a captive portal: Web Policy with web authentication (users log in) or web passthrough (users accept terms). It suits guest WLANs, often with Layer 2 set to None.

**AAA Servers** picks up to six RADIUS servers from the global list (Security > AAA > RADIUS), tried in order. Without a working one, an 802.1X WLAN rejects everyone.

visual.title: Layer 2 choices
rows: Modern encryption. Leave WPA and TKIP unticked: legacy and deprecated
WPA2-Enterprise: each user authenticates with EAP to the RADIUS servers
WPA2 PSK plus WPA3 SAE, PMF optional
Transition mode, so older clients keep working during a migration

sections.pitfall: Choosing 802.1X when you meant a shared passphrase. The WLAN becomes WPA2-Enterprise, and without a working RADIUS server every client fails. For a passphrase, choose PSK.

activity.title: Move a WLAN to WPA3
activity.prompt: Set up a WLAN for WPA3-Personal in the simulated controller: pick the right security options, set a passphrase and make sure the remaining settings WPA3 depends on are correct, then test whether the client can join.

check.question: Which Authentication Key Management choice turns a WPA2 WLAN into WPA2-Personal with a shared passphrase?
check.explanation: PSK uses one pre-shared key for everyone, which is WPA2-Personal. 802.1X makes it WPA2-Enterprise with per-user RADIUS authentication, and web passthrough is a Layer 3 captive portal option.

sections.title: The QoS and Advanced tabs
sections.key: The QoS profile caps a WLAN's priority (Platinum voice, Gold video, Silver best effort by default, Bronze background); Advanced holds a 1800-second session timeout and 60-second client exclusion.
sections.body:
**QoS tab.** The Quality of Service drop-down sets the WLAN's **QoS profile**, the highest priority its traffic gets:

[[visual]]

The same tab sets **WMM** (Wi-Fi Multimedia: Disabled, Allowed or Required), which voice clients need.

**Advanced tab.** Most options are beyond the CCNA, but know these defaults:

[[visual 2]]

Click Apply on each tab. One more default bites administrators: the controller refuses management sessions from wireless clients until **Management > Mgmt Via Wireless** is enabled.

visual.title: QoS profiles
rows: Background, such as a guest WLAN

visual.title: Advanced tab
rows: Blocks clients that keep failing association, authentication or web auth, or reuse another client's IP
Lets RADIUS assign a per-user VLAN, QoS level or ACL
Clients must use DHCP; a static address cannot pass traffic
Stops clients talking directly to each other (good for guests)
Reports areas where clients have a weak signal

sections.pitfall: Expecting a RADIUS VLAN assignment to work on its own. Unless Allow AAA Override is ticked, the controller ignores the VLAN that RADIUS returns and keeps the WLAN's interface.

activity.title: Explore the controller
activity.prompt: Open the simulated controller and walk every tab of a WLAN: find the radio policy, the interface binding, the Layer 2 security settings, the QoS profile and the session timeout. Predict each default before you look.

check.question: A WLAN will carry IP phone calls. Which QoS profile should it use?
check.explanation: Platinum is the voice profile. Gold is for video, Silver is the best-effort default and Bronze is background.

sections.title: The Catalyst 9800 GUI and troubleshooting a WLAN
sections.key: A Catalyst 9800 splits a WLAN into a WLAN profile (SSID, security) and a policy profile (VLAN, QoS, timeouts), joined by a policy tag assigned to the APs.
sections.body:
Catalyst 9800 controllers use the same settings, split into reusable objects under **Configuration > Tags & Profiles**:

[[visual]]

Every AP has exactly one policy, site and RF tag, starting with default-policy-tag, default-site-tag and default-rf-tag. The default policy tag maps WLAN IDs 1 to 16 to default-policy-profile.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

When a client cannot connect, walk the same checks on either GUI:

[[visual 4]]

rows: What the client sees: profile name, SSID, WLAN ID, status, radio policy, broadcast SSID, and security (WPA2 or WPA3, AES, PSK, 802.1X or SAE, PMF, web auth, AAA)
What happens to traffic: the VLAN, QoS (platinum to bronze), central or local switching, session and idle timeouts, exclusion, DHCP required, AAA override
Maps each WLAN profile to a policy profile; APs broadcast only the WLANs in their policy tag
The AP join profile, and local or FlexConnect

visual.title: AireOS setting, 9800 home
rows: General: SSID, status, radio policy, broadcast SSID
Advanced: session timeout, exclusion, AAA override, DHCP required
Policy tag (plus site and RF tags)

steps.label: Is the WLAN enabled and on the client's band?
Is it on the client's AP?
steps.detail: AireOS: the AP's group. 9800: the AP's policy tag

steps.label: Does the security match the client?
steps.detail: PSK or 802.1X, WPA2 or WPA3, PMF

steps.label: For 802.1X: are RADIUS servers defined and reachable?
Is the WLAN mapped to the right VLAN, with DHCP there?
Is the client excluded after failed attempts?

sections.tip: Changing the policy tag on a 9800 AP makes it rejoin the controller, which takes about a minute; plan it for a maintenance window.
sections.pitfall: Creating a 9800 WLAN profile and policy profile and wondering why no AP broadcasts the SSID. Nothing happens until a policy tag maps them and is assigned to the APs (or the WLAN ID is 1 to 16, covered by the default tag).

activity.title: Why can't the client join?
activity.prompt: A WLAN in the simulated controller is not working for the test client. Walk the checklist from this section tab by tab, find every setting that is wrong, fix it and run the client test again.

check.question: On a Catalyst 9800, where do you set the VLAN that a WLAN's clients are placed in?
choices: In the WLAN profile's General tab
In the policy profile, which a policy tag links to the WLAN
In the site tag's AP join profile
check.explanation: The 9800 splits AireOS settings: the WLAN profile holds the SSID and security, the policy profile holds the VLAN, QoS and timeouts, and the policy tag ties the two together for a set of APs. RF and site tags handle radio and AP join settings.

keyTerms.definition: A self-contained AP configured individually; it maps SSIDs to VLANs itself and usually connects to a trunk.
An AP managed from a vendor cloud dashboard (Cisco Meraki); management goes to the cloud, client data stays local.
An AP that performs only real-time 802.11 functions and depends on a WLC for management.
Wireless LAN controller: centrally manages lightweight APs, RF, security, roaming and WLAN configuration.
Dividing 802.11 MAC duties between the AP (real time) and the WLC (management).
Tunneling protocol between lightweight APs and a WLC: control on UDP 5246 (encrypted), data on UDP 5247.
AP mode for branches that can switch client traffic locally and keep working if the WLC is unreachable.
A WLC logical interface that maps a WLAN to a wired VLAN, with its own IP address and DHCP settings.
Link aggregation group: WLC distribution system ports bundled as one link; the switch side uses EtherChannel mode on.
Power over Ethernet: the switch powers the AP over the data cable (802.3af about 15 W, 802.3at about 30 W).
A WLAN's priority level on the WLC: Platinum voice, Gold video, Silver best effort (default), Bronze background.
WLC port for out-of-band management and recovery; supports one VLAN and connects to an access port.
WLC data port carrying CAPWAP, client and in-band management traffic; connects to an 802.1Q trunk.
Wi-Fi Multimedia: 802.11 priority queuing that voice and video clients need; set per WLAN on the QoS tab.
WLAN option that lets the RADIUS server assign a VLAN, QoS level or ACL per user.
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: the WPA3-Personal key exchange that replaces the WPA2 PSK handshake.
Protected Management Frames (802.11w): required by WPA3, optional for WPA2.
Catalyst 9800 object holding a WLAN's VLAN, QoS policy, switching mode and timeouts.
Catalyst 9800 object that maps WLAN profiles to policy profiles; APs broadcast only the WLANs in their policy tag.

summary: Autonomous APs are standalone and trunked; cloud-based APs are managed from the cloud with local data; lightweight APs need a WLC.
Split MAC: real-time work on the AP, management on the WLC, joined by CAPWAP (control UDP 5246, data UDP 5247).
Local mode serves clients, FlexConnect suits branches, and monitor, sniffer, rogue detector and SE-Connect are tools.
Local-mode APs use access ports; autonomous and FlexConnect APs and WLC distribution ports use trunks; AireOS LAG needs mode on.
AireOS WLAN tabs: General (status, radio policy, interface), Security (PSK, 802.1X, SAE with PMF), QoS (Platinum to Bronze), Advanced (1800 s, 60 s, AAA override).
Catalyst 9800: WLAN profile plus policy profile, joined by a policy tag assigned to the APs.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a colleague how a lightweight AP and a WLC share the work of a wireless network, how the AP and WLC plug into switches, and which settings decide a client's VLAN, security and QoS, first on an AireOS controller and then on a Catalyst 9800.

questions.question: Which device does a lightweight AP depend on for its configuration and most management functions?
questions.explanation: Lightweight APs handle only real-time 802.11 work and rely on a WLC, reached over CAPWAP, for configuration, RF management, authentication and policy.

questions.question: In a Cisco Meraki cloud-managed wireless network, where does client data traffic go?
choices: Through a tunnel to the Meraki cloud, then back to the LAN
Through CAPWAP to a WLC in the data center
Directly from the AP onto the local wired network; only management goes to the cloud
Through the nearest autonomous AP acting as a gateway
questions.explanation: Cloud-based APs are managed and monitored from the cloud, but they forward user data locally like autonomous APs. Only control and management traffic reaches the dashboard.

questions.question: Which two statements describe autonomous APs? (Choose two.)
choices: Each AP is configured and managed individually
They tunnel client traffic to a WLC with CAPWAP
Their switch port is usually a trunk carrying the SSIDs' VLANs
They cannot serve clients without a WLC
They cannot be managed with a web browser
questions.explanation: Autonomous APs hold their own configuration and put client traffic onto VLANs themselves, so they need trunks. They work without a WLC and support CLI, HTTP and HTTPS management.

questions.question: Which UDP port carries the CAPWAP control tunnel?
questions.explanation: CAPWAP control uses UDP 5246 and is always protected with DTLS. Client data uses UDP 5247.

questions.question: Which UDP port carries the CAPWAP data tunnel?
questions.explanation: The data tunnel uses UDP 5247. Unlike the control tunnel, it is not encrypted unless DTLS data encryption is enabled.

questions.question: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Tunneling protocol between lightweight APs and a WLC
AP does real-time 802.11 work, WLC does management
Encryption protecting the CAPWAP control tunnel
Older Cisco protocol that CAPWAP is based on
Hands APs the IP addresses of WLCs

questions.explanation: These are the building blocks of a controller-based WLAN: the architecture (split MAC), the tunnel (CAPWAP, from LWAPP), its protection (DTLS) and one way APs find controllers (option 43).

questions.question: In a split-MAC architecture, which three functions does the WLC perform? (Choose three.)
choices: RF management, such as choosing channels and transmit power
Encrypting each 802.11 frame over the air
questions.explanation: Management functions (RF, authentication, roaming, security policy, QoS) move to the WLC. Beacons, probe responses and per-frame encryption are real-time tasks that stay on the AP.

questions.question: A lightweight AP at 10.10.10.10 and its WLC at 10.1.1.5 are in different subnets in different buildings. What is true?
choices: The AP must be moved into the WLC's subnet
A trunk must extend the WLC's VLAN to the AP
The AP must be converted to autonomous mode
The AP can join, because CAPWAP tunnels are IP packets that are simply routed
questions.explanation: CAPWAP encapsulates everything in IP between the AP and the WLC, so Layer 3 routing carries it. That independence from Layer 2 is a major advantage of the design.

questions.question: Put the steps in order for a new lightweight AP coming online.
items: The AP boots and gets an IP address, usually by DHCP
The AP discovers WLC addresses (DHCP option 43, DNS, broadcast or a stored address)
The AP joins a WLC over CAPWAP
The WLC provides software and configuration to the AP
The AP starts advertising its SSIDs to clients
questions.explanation: An AP needs an address before it can find a controller, must join before it receives its configuration, and serves clients only once configured.

questions.question: Which WLC deployment model runs the controller as a virtual machine in a data center?
questions.explanation: A cloud-based WLC is a virtual controller in a data center or private cloud. Unified uses a central hardware appliance, embedded runs in a switch stack and Mobility Express runs on an AP.

questions.question: Match each WLC deployment model to its location and typical scale.

pairs.right: Central hardware controller, about 6000 APs
Virtual machine in a data center, about 3000 APs
Inside an access switch stack, about 200 APs
Running on an AP at a branch, about 100 APs

questions.explanation: The models trade scale for location: the further the controller sits from the core, the fewer APs it typically supports.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a cloud-based WLC deployment from a cloud-based AP architecture?
choices: They are two names for the same design
A cloud-based WLC is a virtual controller still using CAPWAP; cloud-based APs have no WLC and are managed from the vendor's cloud
Cloud-based APs tunnel all client data to the cloud, while a cloud-based WLC does not
A cloud-based WLC manages only autonomous APs
questions.explanation: A cloud-based WLC is a controller VM in your own data center with CAPWAP tunnels to lightweight APs. Meraki-style cloud APs need no WLC; the vendor's cloud manages them, and their data stays local.

questions.question: What is the default mode of a Cisco lightweight AP?
questions.explanation: Local mode is the default: the AP serves clients, tunnels their traffic to the WLC and scans other channels in its spare time.

questions.question: Match each AP mode to its purpose.

pairs.right: Never transmits; dedicated rogue and IDS sensor
Sends captured 802.11 frames to an analyzer
Spectrum analysis to find non-Wi-Fi interference
Correlates wired MACs with rogues heard over the air
Links buildings or forms a mesh
Switches traffic locally at a branch

questions.explanation: Each special mode dedicates the AP to one job. Only FlexConnect (and local) keep serving clients; bridge mode links networks.

questions.question: Users near a break room lose Wi-Fi performance at lunchtime, and you suspect a microwave oven. Which AP mode helps you find non-802.11 interference?
questions.explanation: SE-Connect dedicates the radios to spectrum analysis, which reveals non-Wi-Fi energy such as microwave ovens. A sniffer captures only 802.11 frames, so it cannot see the oven.

questions.question: An engineer needs an AP to capture wireless frames on one channel and send them to a laptop running Wireshark. Which AP mode should be used?
questions.explanation: Sniffer mode forwards captured 802.11 frames to a PC running an analyzer. Monitor mode feeds the WLC's rogue and IDS functions instead of a packet capture tool.

questions.question: Which two AP modes let an AP continue serving wireless clients? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Local and FlexConnect both provide BSSs for clients. Monitor, sniffer and SE-Connect dedicate the radios to a tool function and stop serving clients.

questions.question: Which WLC port connects to a switch trunk and carries CAPWAP tunnels and client traffic?
questions.explanation: Distribution system ports carry all normal traffic in many VLANs, so they connect to 802.1Q trunks. The service port is for out-of-band management on one VLAN.

questions.question: Which WLC port is used for out-of-band management and system recovery and connects to a switch access port?
questions.explanation: The service port supports a single VLAN for out-of-band management and recovery, so its switch port is in access mode. 'Virtual' is a logical interface, not a port.

questions.question: These switch ports connect to an AireOS WLC whose distribution system ports are configured as a LAG. The bundle never forms. What is wrong?
questions.code:
interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/47 - 48
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 50,100,200
 channel-group 5 mode active
choices: A WLC LAG requires PAgP desirable on the switch
WLC distribution system ports must connect to access ports
The AireOS WLC does not negotiate LACP, so the switch ports need channel-group 5 mode on
The allowed VLAN list must include VLAN 1
questions.explanation: AireOS controllers support only static link aggregation. The switch must use mode on; LACP active waits forever for a partner that never answers.

questions.question: Why does a lightweight AP in local mode need only an access port, even when its WLANs map to several different VLANs?
choices: All WLAN traffic travels inside the CAPWAP tunnel to the WLC, which connects to those VLANs
The AP converts every WLAN into the native VLAN
Wireless frames carry no VLAN information
The access port automatically becomes a trunk when PoE is used
questions.explanation: The AP needs only its own IP address to build CAPWAP tunnels. The WLC, connected to the VLANs through trunked distribution ports, places each WLAN's traffic in its VLAN.

questions.question: Match each WLC logical interface to its role.

pairs.right: Terminates CAPWAP and handles management traffic
Non-routed address for client DHCP relay and web auth
Maps a WLAN to a wired VLAN
Out-of-band management through the service port

questions.explanation: Interfaces are logical Layer 3 terminations inside the WLC, distinct from the physical ports that connect it to switches.

questions.question: About how many watts per port does 802.3at (PoE+) supply at the switch? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: PoE+ (802.3at) supplies up to about 30 W at the switch port, double the roughly 15 W of 802.3af PoE. Newer 802.3bt (UPOE) supplies 60 W or more.

questions.question: In the AireOS WLC GUI, where do you start creating a new WLAN?
questions.explanation: The WLANs tab lists WLANs and offers Create New. Controller > Interfaces is where dynamic interfaces are created, and Security > AAA is where RADIUS servers are defined.

questions.question: Before creating a WLAN that should place clients in VLAN 100, what should you create under Controller > Interfaces?
choices: A dynamic interface with VLAN ID 100, an IP address and DHCP server addresses
A RADIUS server entry for VLAN 100
questions.explanation: A dynamic interface connects the WLC to a wired VLAN. The WLAN's General tab then binds the WLAN to that interface.

questions.question: A WLAN is fully configured, but the Status check box on its General tab is not ticked. What happens?
choices: Clients can join but get no IP address
The WLAN exists but is not advertised or usable
The SSID is hidden but clients can still join
The WLAN is offered only on 2.4 GHz radios
questions.explanation: Status enables or disables the WLAN. A disabled WLAN is kept in the configuration but not pushed to the APs' radios. Hiding the SSID is the separate Broadcast SSID setting.

questions.question: A WLAN uses Layer 2 Security WPA+WPA2 with WPA2 Policy and AES, and Authentication Key Management is set to 802.1X. No RADIUS server is defined. Users who type the correct shared passphrase cannot join. What is the fix?
choices: Change Authentication Key Management to PSK and set the passphrase
Change the QoS profile to Platinum
questions.explanation: 802.1X makes the WLAN WPA2-Enterprise, which authenticates each user against RADIUS, so a shared passphrase is never used. PSK makes it WPA2-Personal. (Alternatively, keep 802.1X and add working RADIUS servers and user accounts.)

questions.question: Match each WLC QoS profile to the traffic it is meant for.

pairs.right: Voice
Video
Best effort (the default)
Background

questions.explanation: The metals rank priority from Platinum (voice) down to Bronze (background). New WLANs default to Silver.

questions.question: What is the default WLAN session timeout on an AireOS WLC, in seconds?
questions.explanation: Client sessions are limited to 1800 seconds (30 minutes) by default, after which clients must reauthenticate. It is set on the Advanced tab.

questions.question: Which two Layer 2 security options should be avoided on a new WLAN because they are weak or deprecated? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: WEP is broken and WPA with TKIP is deprecated. WPA2 with AES is the baseline, and WPA3 with SAE is the stronger current option.

questions.question: A guest WLAN must stop guests from reaching each other's laptops over Wi-Fi. Which Advanced tab setting helps most?
questions.explanation: P2P (peer-to-peer) blocking prevents clients on the same WLAN from communicating directly. AAA Override lets RADIUS assign per-user settings, and the other two do not control client-to-client traffic.

questions.question: Explain the split-MAC architecture in two or three sentences.
questions.answer: The 802.11 MAC functions are divided between the lightweight AP and the WLC. The AP keeps the real-time work (sending and receiving frames, beacons, probe responses, encryption), while the WLC does management (RF tuning, authentication, roaming, security and QoS). The two communicate through CAPWAP tunnels.
questions.explanation: Putting management on the controller is what lets one WLC configure and tune hundreds of APs at once.

questions.question: Newer laptops join the Engineering WLAN without trouble, but an older laptop with only a 2.4 GHz radio never even sees the SSID. Based on the WLAN's General tab, what is the cause?
questions.code:
WLANs > Edit 'Engineering'      [General] [Security] [QoS] [Advanced]

  Profile Name               Engineering
  SSID                       Engineering
  Status                     [x] Enabled
  Security Policies          [WPA2][Auth(PSK)]
  Radio Policy               802.11a only
  Interface/Interface Group  engineering
  Broadcast SSID             [x] Enabled
choices: The Radio Policy offers the WLAN only on 5 GHz (802.11a) radios
The WLAN is bound to the wrong dynamic interface
WPA2 PSK is not supported on 2.4 GHz
questions.explanation: 802.11a only advertises the WLAN on the 5 GHz radios, so a 2.4 GHz-only client never hears its beacons. Setting Radio Policy to All (or including 802.11b/g) fixes it. Broadcast SSID is enabled, and the interface affects VLAN placement, not visibility.

questions.question: Clients on the Engineering WLAN connect and authenticate, but they receive addresses from 10.10.10.0/24, the WLC management subnet, instead of the engineering VLAN 100 subnet. Based on the settings, what should be changed?
questions.code:
Controller > Interfaces
  Interface Name   VLAN Identifier   IP Address       Interface Type
  engineering      100               192.168.100.10   Dynamic
  management       10                10.10.10.5       Static
  virtual          N/A               192.0.2.1        Static

WLANs > Edit 'Engineering' > General
  Interface/Interface Group  management
  Status                     [x] Enabled
choices: Change the WLAN's Interface/Interface Group to engineering
Change the virtual interface address to 192.168.100.1
Set the QoS profile to Gold
Enable AAA Override on the Advanced tab
questions.explanation: The WLAN is still bound to the default management interface, so client traffic lands in VLAN 10. Binding it to the engineering dynamic interface puts clients in VLAN 100, where its DHCP settings apply. The virtual interface is only for client-facing services such as DHCP relay.

questions.question: An AireOS administrator moving to a Catalyst 9800 asks where the WLAN's Interface/Interface Group setting went. What is the answer?
choices: It is the VLAN in the policy profile, linked to the WLAN by a policy tag
It is the WLAN ID field on the WLAN profile
It moved to the RF tag
The 9800 always uses the management VLAN for clients
questions.explanation: On the 9800 the VLAN lives in the policy profile (Access Policies tab), and a policy tag links the WLAN profile to that policy profile. The WLAN profile keeps the SSID, security and radio settings.

questions.question: Match each Catalyst 9800 configuration object to what it holds.

pairs.right: SSID, WLAN ID and security settings
VLAN, QoS policy and session timeout
Maps each WLAN profile to a policy profile
AP join profile and local or FlexConnect mode
RF profiles for each band

questions.explanation: WLAN profile is what clients see, policy profile is what happens to their traffic, the policy tag joins them, and site and RF tags carry AP join and radio settings. Every AP gets one of each tag.

questions.question: On a Catalyst 9800 an engineer created WLAN profile CORP with WLAN ID 20 and a policy profile CORP-POLICY with VLAN 100. The APs, which still use default-policy-tag, do not broadcast CORP. What is missing?
choices: The WLAN must be enabled under the RF tag
A policy tag that maps CORP to CORP-POLICY, assigned to the APs
Broadcast SSID must be set in the policy profile
questions.explanation: APs broadcast only WLANs in their policy tag. The default policy tag maps only WLAN IDs 1 to 16, to the default policy profile, so WLAN 20 is in no tag. Create a policy tag that maps CORP to CORP-POLICY and assign it to the APs.

questions.question: Which combination configures a WLAN for WPA3-Personal?
choices: WPA2 Policy with TKIP and PSK
WPA3 Policy with 802.1X and PMF disabled
WPA3 Policy with SAE and PMF Required
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal replaces PSK key exchange with SAE and requires Protected Management Frames. 802.1X would make it Enterprise, and TKIP is a deprecated WPA option that WPA3 does not use.

questions.question: Which three settings are on the General tab of an AireOS WLAN? (Choose three.)
questions.explanation: The General tab holds Status, Radio Policy, the Interface/Interface Group binding, Broadcast SSID and the profile name and SSID. The QoS profile has its own tab, and the PSK is set on the Security tab.

questions.question: Put the AireOS steps in order to create a WPA2-Enterprise WLAN for VLAN 100.
items: Add the RADIUS server under Security > AAA > RADIUS > Authentication
Create a dynamic interface for VLAN 100 under Controller > Interfaces
Choose WLANs > Create New and enter the profile name and SSID
On the General tab, enable the WLAN and bind it to the dynamic interface
On the Security tab, choose WPA2 with 802.1X and select the RADIUS server
Click Apply to save the WLAN
questions.explanation: Define the RADIUS server and the dynamic interface first, because the WLAN refers to both. Then create the WLAN, bind its interface and enable it, choose 802.1X security and the AAA servers, and apply.

questions.question: An administrator on the corporate Wi-Fi cannot open the WLC GUI, but the same laptop works when plugged into a wired port. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The WLC GUI only supports HTTP
The WLAN uses the Silver QoS profile
Management through wireless is disabled by default on the controller
questions.explanation: By default a WLC refuses management sessions from wireless clients. Enabling Management > Mgmt Via Wireless allows them. The GUI itself is fine, as the wired test shows.

questions.question: A barcode scanner with a static IP address associates and authenticates to the WAREHOUSE WLAN but cannot pass any traffic. Laptops using DHCP work. Based on the Advanced tab, what is the cause?
questions.code:
WLANs > Edit 'WAREHOUSE' > Advanced
  Allow AAA Override            [ ] Enabled
  Enable Session Timeout        [x] 1800 seconds
  Client Exclusion              [x] Enabled   Timeout Value 60 seconds
  DHCP Addr. Assignment         [x] Required
  P2P Blocking Action           Disabled
choices: Client exclusion has blocked the scanner for 60 seconds
DHCP Addr. Assignment Required blocks clients that did not get their address by DHCP
The session timeout is too short for scanners
P2P blocking prevents the scanner from reaching the server
questions.explanation: With DHCP Addr. Assignment Required, the controller passes traffic only for clients that obtained an address through DHCP. A statically addressed client never completes DHCP, so it is blocked. Untick the option or give the scanner a DHCP reservation.

questions.question: For how many seconds does an AireOS WLC exclude a client that repeatedly fails authentication, by default? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: Client Exclusion is enabled by default with a 60-second timeout, a short deterrent against password guessing and misbehaving clients.

questions.question: A guest WLAN must send users to a web page where they accept the terms of use before they get internet access. Where is that configured?
choices: Security > Layer 2, Authentication Key Management PSK
questions.explanation: A captive portal is Layer 3 security: Security > Layer 3 with a web policy (web passthrough for accepting terms, web authentication for a login). Layer 2 is often None for such guest WLANs.

questions.question: ISE returns VLAN 30 for members of the contractors group, but contractors on the CORP WLAN keep landing in VLAN 100, the WLAN's own interface VLAN. Authentication succeeds. What should be changed on the WLAN?
choices: Change the QoS profile to Gold
Set the radio policy to 802.11a only
questions.explanation: The controller applies attributes returned by RADIUS, such as a VLAN, only when Allow AAA Override is enabled on the WLAN (on a 9800, in the policy profile). Without it, every client gets the WLAN's configured VLAN.
